summary: Singapore has no forced heirship: non-Muslims may leave their estate freely, with family members able to apply for provision. Muslims follow Islamic shares and can will one third. Trusts are well developed and Hague-style recognition is in the Recognition of Trusts Act, but the Convention itself is not in force and there is no foundation law.
family_claims: Spouse, children and certain dependants may apply for provision under the Inheritance (Family Provision) Act 1966. Muslims: Administration of Muslim Law Act 1966, fixed shares and a one-third will limit.
foreign_law_note: Common-law conflict rules: movables follow the law of domicile at death, immovables follow the law of their location. A foreigner domiciled abroad keeps foreign law for movables. A foreigner domiciled in Singapore is under Singapore law. Estate duty has been abolished since 15 February 2008.
trust_note: Not on the HCCH status table, but the Recognition of Trusts Act 2004 recognises trusts governed by foreign law on Hague terms. Trusts are under the Trustees Act 1967 and the Trust Companies Act 2005. Singapore has no foundation statute; families use trusts, companies limited by guarantee and the variable capital company.
open_questions: Statute names were taken from the Rajah & Tann chapter and knowledge; confirm the current Act titles on Singapore Statutes Online.
Confirm no private foundation legislation is pending.
